subject: English
description: Tricky cases — collective nouns, either/or, neither/nor, indefinite pronouns, intervening phrases

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The committee ___ on the proposal next week.'
questions.explanation: COLLECTIVE NOUNS like committee, government, jury, team take SINGULAR verb when acting as a unit; PLURAL when members act individually. Here 'committee' acts as a unit → singular 'is deciding'. Distractor 1 — plural 'are' would be valid only if members are acting individually. Distractor 3 — 'have' is plural. Distractor 4 — 'were' is plural and 'decided' would be passive past.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Neither the manager nor the staff ___ ready for the inspection.'
questions.explanation: RULE: With 'either/or' and 'neither/nor', the verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST to it (the proximity rule). Here 'staff' (treated as plural) is nearest → plural verb 'are'. If reversed: 'Neither the staff nor the manager IS ready' would use singular. Distractor 1 — 'is' would match 'manager' (further from verb), wrong. Distractors 3, 4 — wrong tense/aspect.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Each of the players ___ given a uniform.'
questions.explanation: RULE: 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither', 'none', 'one' are SINGULAR — take a singular verb, even when followed by a plural noun. 'Each of the players IS given'. Distractor 1 'are' is the common mistake (eyes track 'players'). Distractor 3 'have been' is plural. Distractor 4 'were' is plural past.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The teacher, along with her students, ___ visiting the museum.'
questions.explanation: Phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'in addition to', 'including' do NOT change the number of the subject. Subject = 'teacher' (singular) → singular verb 'is'. Compare with 'and' which DOES create a plural compound subject. Distractor 1 'are' wrongly responds to 'students'. Distractor 3 'have been' is plural. Distractor 4 'were' is plural past.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'A pair of shoes ___ kept in the wardrobe.'
questions.explanation: 'Pair of' is grammatically singular as the subject (pair = one set of two items). 'A pair of shoes IS kept'. Similarly: 'a couple of friends' (singular when treating couple as unit). Distractor 1 'are' tracks 'shoes' but shoes is the OBJECT of 'of'. Distractor 3 — also passive but uses 'has been', incorrect with 'kept'. Distractor 4 'have' is plural.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The number of accidents on this highway ___ rising every year.'
questions.explanation: 'THE number of' — singular (refers to one specific count). Takes singular verb. CONTRAST: 'A number of' — plural (means 'several/many'). Examples: 'The number of cars IS rising' vs 'A number of cars ARE parked'. Distractor 1 'are' would be correct only with 'a number of'. Distractors 3, 4 are plural / wrong tense.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Mathematics ___ my favourite subject in school.'
questions.explanation: Subject names ending in -s — Mathematics, Physics, Statistics, Economics, Politics, News, Measles — are GRAMMATICALLY SINGULAR despite the -s ending. 'Mathematics is fascinating'. CONTRAST: 'his politics are confusing' (politics as views/opinions, not subject). Distractor 1 'are' wrongly treats 'mathematics' as plural. Distractors 3, 4 are also plural/wrong.
